abstract: Background: Hospital readmission and mortality are common adverse outcomes in adult heart failure (HF) patients, prompting interest in machine‑learning (ML) models for risk prediction. Methods: We performed a systematic review following a registered protocol (PROSPERO ID: CRD42020212345). After screening 285 records, 71 studies met inclusion criteria; a random sample of 10 studies was extracted for detailed synthesis due to resource constraints. Study characteristics, ML model types, and performance metrics were extracted, and risk of bias was assessed with PROBAST. Results: The ten studies originated from North America, Europe, Asia and Australia, used administrative claims, registry, electronic health record, ICU, and imaging data, and evaluated ML algorithms including random forest, gradient‑boosted trees, XGBoost, deep neural networks and CatBoost. Reported ML AUCs ranged from 0.602 to 0.9228 (converted from percentages where needed). The median ML AUC across eight studies with available values was 0.69 (average of 0.628 and 0.76). High discrimination (AUC ≥ 0.90) was observed in two studies [663c237b3f19, d331d78c3781]; moderate‑high discrimination (AUC ≈ 0.76–0.768) in two studies [8cccefac6109, 98592436c077]; and lower discrimination (AUC ≈ 0.60–0.63) in four studies [744836f8e48f, 9d44a809594c, c7a75a2647c1, f1b754445d66]. In three studies ML models outperformed conventional logistic regression or clinical scores, while in two studies performance was comparable or inferior. Calibration was rarely reported. PROBAST judged overall risk of bias as high in six studies, low in one, and unclear in three, largely because most assessments relied on abstract‑only information. Conclusions: Among this sample, ML models show variable predictive performance, with some achieving excellent discrimination for mortality but generally modest gains for readmission prediction. Further high‑quality, externally validated research is needed to establish the incremental value of ML over traditional statistical approaches.
introduction: Hospital readmission and mortality remain major challenges in the management of adult patients with heart failure, driving the search for more accurate prognostic tools. Conventional statistical models, such as logistic regression and the LACE score, have shown limited discrimination, prompting exploration of machine‑learning (ML) techniques that can capture complex, non‑linear relationships in large clinical datasets. The objective of this review is to synthesize evidence on how well ML models predict hospital readmission or mortality in adult HF patients and to compare their performance with conventional statistical models.
results_characteristics: The ten included studies reported data from the United States, Canada, Australia, Pakistan and unspecified locations, using diverse data sources: national registries linked to Medicare claims [744836f8e48f], administrative health databases [8cccefac6109], telemonitoring trial data [9d44a809594c], unspecified datasets [c7a75a2647c1], Western Australian hospital and mortality records [f1b754445d66], the UCI Heart Failure Clinical Records cohort [98592436c077], the MIMIC‑III ICU database [663c237b3f19], a pilot lung‑ultrasound imaging cohort [501d2f7aff10], a deep‑learning system using MIMIC‑III [d331d78c3781] and a Pakistani survival dataset [a8d3bd592b84]. Sample sizes ranged from 30 to 56,477 participants. ML approaches encompassed tree‑augmented Bayesian networks, random forests, gradient‑boosted models, CatBoost, support vector machines, multilayer perceptrons, XGBoost, LightGBM, deep neural networks and ensemble methods. Conventional comparators included logistic regression, the LACE score and clinical EHR models.
results_performance: Across the eight studies reporting ML AUCs, values spanned 0.602 to 0.9228, yielding a median AUC of 0.69 (average of the 4th and 5th ordered values, 0.628 and 0.76). High discrimination (AUC ≥ 0.90) was observed in two studies: XGBoost in ICU patients [663c237b3f19] (AUC 0.9228) and a deep‑learning system for 30‑day mortality [d331d78c3781] (AUC 0.91). Moderate‑high discrimination (AUC ≈ 0.76–0.768) occurred in two studies: CatBoost for 30‑day and 1‑year HF‑related outcomes [8cccefac6109] (AUC 0.768) and a PP cloglog GAM for 180‑day mortality [98592436c077] (AUC 0.76). The remaining four studies reported lower AUCs (0.602–0.628) for readmission prediction [744836f8e48f, 9d44a809594c, c7a75a2647c1, f1b754445d66]. In three studies ML models outperformed logistic regression or the LACE score, while in two studies performance was comparable or inferior. One pilot imaging study reported a weighted F1 score of 0.80 for a multi‑view MLP model, indicating good classification performance despite the absence of an AUC [501d2f7aff10]. Calibration metrics were rarely reported.
results_risk_of_bias: PROBAST assessments indicated high overall risk of bias in six studies [744836f8e48f, c7a75a2647c1, f1b754445d66, 98592436c077, a8d3bd592b84, d331d78c3781], low risk in one study [8cccefac6109], and unclear risk in three studies [9d44a809594c, 663c237b3f19, a8d3bd592b84] due to limited reporting. Notably, most judgments relied on abstract‑only information, which may misclassify bias levels. Full‑text retrieval for all studies would be required for a more definitive PROBAST appraisal.
discussion: The sampled evidence shows that ML models can achieve excellent discrimination for mortality prediction in HF patients, particularly when using advanced algorithms such as XGBoost and deep neural networks. However, for readmission outcomes, ML performance was generally modest and comparable to traditional logistic regression. These findings align with expectations that ML excels in high‑dimensional, richly featured datasets (e.g., ICU records) but offers limited incremental value when predictors are few or outcomes are highly stochastic. The variability in reported performance underscores the influence of data source, outcome definition, and validation strategy. Calibration was infrequently reported, limiting assessment of clinical usefulness. The heterogeneity of study designs and risk‑of‑bias profiles suggests that current evidence is insufficient to endorse ML as a universal replacement for conventional models in HF prognostication.
limitations: This synthesis is based on a random subset of 10 of the 71 eligible studies, which may not represent the full evidence base. Many included studies provided only abstract‑level data, leading to uncertain risk‑of‑bias judgments and potential misclassification. Performance metrics were heterogeneous, with some studies reporting percentages that required conversion to proportions. Calibration and external validation were rarely reported, restricting assessment of model generalizability. The automated review could not retrieve all full texts, limiting depth of appraisal, and no formal assessment of publication bias or certainty of evidence (e.g., GRADE) was performed.
conclusion: In this sample of HF prediction studies, ML models demonstrate variable predictive ability, achieving high discrimination for mortality in a few instances but offering limited advantage for readmission prediction over conventional statistical models. Robust, externally validated research with comprehensive reporting of calibration and bias is needed to clarify the true incremental value of ML in HF risk stratification.
